lessons.title: Math is In My World
lessons.objective: I can represent a real-world situation with a tape diagram or table and use decimal operations to solve it.
lessons.languageObjective: I can describe my tool using the words tape diagram, table, and this represents ___ .

concept.heading: Visualize the problem, then choose a tool
concept.intro: The book opens with a warm-up — about how many coins are in the picture? — then rides an aerial tramway that must move 4,000 passengers.
concept.keyIdea: Math Practices: Visual Models & Tools. 1. Select the mathematical tool (tape diagram, number line, grid) that best represents the quantities. 2. Label all parts and units clearly. 3. Connect visual relationships directly to numerical expressions

worked.title: Watch me estimate the coins
lines: A pile of coins is too big to count one at a time. About how many coins are in the pile?
I do not count every coin — I find a small stack I CAN count, about 10 coins.
Then I estimate how many stacks like that are in the pile. I count about 15.
15 stacks of about 10 is 15 × 10 = 150, so my estimate is about 150 coins — reasoned, not random.
linesEs: Un montón de monedas es demasiado grande para contarlo una por una. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas monedas hay en el montón?
No cuento cada moneda — busco una pila pequeña que sí pueda contar, de unas 10 monedas.
Luego estimo cuántas pilas así hay en el montón. Cuento unas 15.
15 pilas de unas 10 son 15 × 10 = 150, así que mi estimación es de unas 150 monedas — razonada, no al azar.

together.title: Let's ride the tram together
lines: One tram ride takes 12.5 minutes, so 10 rides take 12.5 × 10 = 125 minutes and 50 rides take 12.5 × 50 = 625 minutes.
The tram needs 50 rides to move 4,000 passengers, and 625 minutes is 625 ÷ 60 hours — about 10.42 hours.
A tape diagram of 4,000 cut into equal rides shows WHY we divide, and the table shows how minutes grow with rides.
linesEs: Un viaje del teleférico toma 12.5 minutos, así que 10 viajes toman 12.5 × 10 = 125 minutos y 50 viajes toman 12.5 × 50 = 625 minutos.
El teleférico necesita 50 viajes para mover a 4,000 pasajeros, y 625 minutos son 625 ÷ 60 horas — unas 10.42 horas.
Un diagrama de barras de 4,000 repartido en viajes iguales muestra por qué dividimos, y la tabla muestra cómo crecen los minutos con los viajes.

vocabulary.definition: A picture, diagram, table, or equation that shows the mathematics in a situation.
vocabulary.example: The same 12 shown three ways: a tape diagram, a table, and 3 × 4.

vocabulary.definition: A rectangle cut into equal parts that helps you visualize how a total breaks apart.
vocabulary.example: One bar of 4,000 passengers cut into equal groups of 80.

vocabulary.definition: Anything you choose to help you see relationships and solve a problem — a table, a diagram, a graph.
vocabulary.example: A table, a number line, or a tape diagram — whichever shows the relationship.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers that go together, like a time and a number of trips, that you can plot as a point.
vocabulary.example: (4, 60): 4 hours costs $60 — the hours always come first.

vocabulary.definition: A complete journey from the start, to the destination, and back to the start.
vocabulary.example: 5 miles out plus 5 miles back = 10 miles in all.

lessons.title: Math is Explaining and Sharing
lessons.objective: I can construct an argument using equations, drawings, or words, and use volume to defend a recommendation.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my thinking with clear math vocabulary using the words argument, conjecture, and cubic units.

concept.heading: When we do math, we develop arguments to defend our thinking
concept.intro: Getting an answer is only half the work. The other half is explaining it so clearly — with conjectures, examples, and counterexamples — that someone else can decide whether your argument is convincing.
concept.keyIdea: Math Practices: Mathematical Arguments & Justification. 1. State a clear claim or conjecture supported by calculations. 2. Use accurate units and vocabulary (e.g. cubic units for volume). 3. Test with counterexamples to verify that the rule holds true every time

worked.title: Watch me argue with equations
lines: Suppose each large box is 8 inches long, 3 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. Its volume is 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches, so three large boxes hold 240 × 3 = 720 cubic inches.
Suppose each jumbo box is 10 inches long, 4 inches wide, and 10 inches tall. Its volume is 10 × 4 × 10 = 400 cubic inches, so two jumbo boxes hold 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches.
I recommend buying two jumbo boxes because 800 cubic inches is greater than 720 cubic inches — the total volume is greater, so there is more cereal for the same price.
linesEs: Supongamos que cada caja grande mide 8 pulgadas de largo, 3 de ancho y 10 de alto. Su volumen es 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 pulgadas cúbicas, así que tres cajas grandes contienen 240 × 3 = 720 pulgadas cúbicas.
Supongamos que cada caja jumbo mide 10 pulgadas de largo, 4 de ancho y 10 de alto. Su volumen es 10 × 4 × 10 = 400 pulgadas cúbicas, así que dos cajas jumbo contienen 400 × 2 = 800 pulgadas cúbicas.
Recomiendo comprar dos cajas jumbo porque 800 pulgadas cúbicas es más que 720 pulgadas cúbicas — el volumen total es mayor, así que hay más cereal por el mismo precio.

together.title: Let's argue with words together
lines: Not every good reason is an equation. Finish this argument: “I recommend buying two jumbo boxes because …”
The book offers two word-based reasons: there is less packaging with two boxes, and two boxes are easier to store than three boxes.

Now listen to the other side. One student recommends the three large boxes because the cereal will stay fresher — each box is open for less time — and because greater volume does not always mean more cereal inside.
How convincing is each argument? That judgment is math too.
linesEs: No toda buena razón es una ecuación. Termina este argumento: «Recomiendo comprar dos cajas jumbo porque…»
El libro ofrece dos razones con palabras: hay menos empaque con dos cajas, y dos cajas son más fáciles de guardar que tres.

Ahora escucha el otro lado. Un estudiante recomienda las tres cajas grandes porque el cereal se mantendrá más fresco — cada caja está abierta menos tiempo — y porque más volumen no siempre significa más cereal adentro.
¿Qué tan convincente es cada argumento? Ese juicio también es matemática.

vocabulary.definition: A chain of reasons — equations, drawings, or words — used to defend your thinking.
vocabulary.example: “Two jumbo boxes hold more, because 400 × 2 = 800 > 720.”

vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement you believe is true but have not yet proven.
vocabulary.example: “A bigger box ALWAYS holds more cereal” — believed, not yet proven.

vocabulary.definition: A single example that shows a statement is not always true.
vocabulary.example: One jumbo box sold half full of air breaks “bigger always holds more”.

vocabulary.definition: The amount of space a solid figure takes up, measured in cubic units.
vocabulary.example: 8 in × 3 in × 10 in = 240 cubic inches of cereal space.

vocabulary.definition: A cube with edges 1 unit long — the unit used to measure volume.
vocabulary.example: One cube, 1 unit on every edge — the block volume is counted in.

title: Neighborhood Makers Market
mission: Plan a tiny market stall. Make sensible money decisions and persuade another designer using a clear model and calculation.
investigate: Predict the cost of four items priced $3.50 before checking.

Explain why changing the number of items changes the total multiplicatively.
create: Plan a stall purchase with a $25 budget. Record the price, quantity, total, and change. Write a convincing explanation of why the plan stays within budget.

support.prompt: One tram ride takes 12.5 minutes. How many minutes do 10 rides take?
support.explanation: 12.5 × 10 = 125. Multiplying by 10 shifts every digit one place to the left.
feedback: 1.25 moves the decimal point the wrong way — that DIVIDES 12.5 by 10.
22.5 ADDS 12.5 + 10 instead of multiplying.
1,250 multiplies by 100 instead of 10.
hints: You need 10 equal groups of 12.5.
Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point one place.
Which direction makes the number bigger?

support.prompt: Five Breaks: which of these is a correct way to decompose 12.5?
support.explanation: 10 + 2.5 = 12.5. The parts of a decomposition must rebuild the number exactly.
feedback: 1 + 2.5 = 3.5 — that drops the tens digit of 12.5.
10 + 2.05 = 12.05 — the 5 slid from the tenths place to the hundredths place.
12 + 5 = 17 — the 5 in 12.5 is five TENTHS, not five ones.
hints: Add each option and compare to 12.5.
What does the 5 in 12.5 stand for?
Add the two parts in each choice, and keep the tenths in mind — 12.5 is 12 and five tenths.

support.prompt: How many minutes do 50 tram rides take, at 12.5 minutes per ride?
support.explanation: 12.5 × 50 = 625, just as the table shows: 1 ride → 12.5, 10 rides → 125, 50 rides → 625.
feedback: 62.5 is 12.5 × 5 — that uses 5 rides instead of 50.
600 is 12 × 50 — it drops the 0.5 in 12.5, losing 25 minutes.
6,250 is 12.5 × 500 — the decimal shifted one place too far.
hints: Use the table pattern: 10 rides take 125 minutes.
50 rides is 5 groups of 10 rides.

support.prompt: Each tram ride carries 80 passengers. How many rides are needed to transport 4,000 passengers?
support.explanation: 4,000 ÷ 80 = 50. A tape diagram of 4,000 cut into equal groups of 80 shows why this is division.
feedback: 500 divides 4,000 by 8 instead of 80 — the zero matters.
3,920 SUBTRACTS 80 from 4,000 — that only unloads one ride.
320,000 MULTIPLIES 4,000 × 80 instead of dividing.
hints: You are splitting 4,000 into equal groups of 80.
Which operation splits a total into equal groups?

support.prompt: A coin display has about 15 stacks that look the same size. You count 10 coins in one stack. About how many coins are in the display? Explain how to estimate without counting every coin.
support.explanation: I counted one small stack of about 10 coins, then estimated that about 15 stacks like it fill the picture, so about 150 coins. An estimate is a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful.

support.prompt: An egg muffin is about 60 calories. A plate holds 4 egg muffins. About how many calories are on the plate?
support.explanation: 4 muffins at about 60 calories each is 60 × 4 = 240 calories.
feedback: That divides 60 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 60 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies 60 by 10 instead of by 4.
hints: How many muffins, and how many calories in each one?
4 equal groups of 60.
Multiply 60 × 4.

support.prompt: A large cereal box is 8 in long, 3 in wide, and 10 in tall. What is its volume?
support.explanation: Volume of a rectangular prism is length × width × height: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches.
feedback: That adds 8 + 3 + 10 instead of multiplying the dimensions.
That multiplies only 8 × 10 and leaves out the 3-inch width.
The number is right, but volume is measured in CUBIC inches — square inches measure area.
hints: Volume of a box is length × width × height.
Multiply 8 × 3 first, then use the height.

support.prompt: Each jumbo box holds 400 cubic inches. How much do TWO jumbo boxes hold?
support.explanation: Two boxes of 400 cubic inches each is 400 × 2 = 800 cubic inches.
feedback: That divides 400 by 2 instead of doubling.
That adds 400 + 2 instead of doubling.
That multiplies 400 by 10 instead of by 2.
hints: Two equal boxes — what operation combines them?
Double 400.

support.prompt: Which unit should the garden group use when reporting how much soil fills the beds?
support.explanation: Volume is measured in cubic units, so soil that fills a space is measured in cubic feet.
feedback: Feet measure length — one dimension, not the space inside the bed.
Square feet measure area — the flat top of the bed, not how deep the soil goes.
Degrees measure angles or temperature, not the space soil fills.
hints: Soil fills SPACE, not a line or a flat surface.
Which unit is for volume?
Volume is measured in cubic units.

support.prompt: Yuzuki can buy three large boxes or two jumbo boxes for the same price. Give ONE reason in words (no equations) for either choice.
support.explanation: I recommend two jumbo boxes because there is less packaging, and two boxes are easier to store than three.

support.prompt: Predict the order total for these settings. Give the answer in dollars. Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: $3.50 × 4 = $14.00. Change from $50: $36.00. A negative result means more money is needed.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: Four supplies cost $3.75 each. What is the total cost in dollars?
support.explanation: 3.75 × 4 = 15.00. Four lots of $0.75 make $3, and four lots of $3 make $12.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: You pay for a $15 order with $25. How much change should you receive?
support.explanation: 25 − 15 = 10 dollars. Check: cost plus change equals the amount paid.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: The 50 rides take 625 minutes. About how many HOURS is that?
core.explanation: 625 ÷ 60 ≈ 10.42, so it would take about 10.42 hours to transport 4,000 passengers.
feedback: 6.25 moves the decimal two places — that divides by 100, but an hour is 60 minutes.
12.5 is the minutes for ONE ride, not the hours for all 50.
62.5 divides by 10 — an hour is 60 minutes, not 10.
hints: How many minutes are in one hour?
Divide the total minutes by 60.

core.prompt: How does the answer change for 2,000 passengers? Each ride carries 80 passengers and takes 12.5 minutes. How many MINUTES are needed?
core.explanation: 2,000 ÷ 80 = 25 rides, and 25 × 12.5 = 312.5 minutes — half the passengers, half the 625 minutes.
feedback: 31.25 shifts the decimal one place left — 25 × 12.5 is more than 25 × 10 = 250.
300 uses 12 minutes per ride instead of 12.5 — the missing 0.5 costs 12.5 minutes across 25 rides.
3,125 shifts the decimal one place right — check with estimation: 25 × 12.5 is close to 25 × 12 = 300.
hints: First find the rides: 2,000 ÷ 80.
That is 25 rides at 12.5 minutes each.

core.prompt: One round trip takes 35 minutes. Using the table (35 → 1, 350 → 10, 525 → 15, 700 → 20), how many round trips does a tram car complete in 10 hours?
core.explanation: 10 hours is 600 minutes. 17 trips take 17 × 35 = 595 minutes, and an 18th trip would need 630 — past the 600. So the tram completes 17 round trips.
feedback: 15 trips is the 525-minute row — that stops 75 minutes early, with time for two more trips.
18 rounds 600 ÷ 35 ≈ 17.1 UP, but the 18th trip is not finished within the 10 hours.
20 trips is the 700-minute row — that is more time than the 600 minutes in 10 hours.
hints: Convert 10 hours to minutes first.
600 minutes falls between the 525 and 700 rows of the table.
600 ÷ 35 is about 17.1 — can a partial trip count as completed?

core.prompt: The round trip is 5 miles. How far does a tram car travel in 5 round trips?
core.explanation: 5 round trips × 5 miles per trip = 25 miles.
feedback: 1 DIVIDES 5 by 5 instead of multiplying.
10 ADDS 5 + 5 instead of multiplying 5 trips by 5 miles.
50 is the distance for 10 round trips, not 5.
hints: Each trip covers the same 5 miles.
You need 5 equal groups of 5 miles.

core.prompt: Compare these tram problems. A: A tram carries 80 passengers per ride and each ride takes 35 minutes. How long would 4,000 passengers take? B: A different tram completes a round trip in 12.5 minutes. How many round trips fit in 10 hours? How are the problems alike and different?
core.explanation: They are the same because both relate time to a number of tram trips and both can use a table of values. They are different because the first starts from passengers and asks for total time, while the second starts from a total time (10 hours) and asks how many round trips fit inside it.

core.prompt: Three large boxes hold 240 cubic inches each. Two jumbo boxes hold 400 cubic inches each. Which is the correct volume comparison?
choices: 240 cubic inches vs. 400 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
480 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the large option holds more
core.explanation: 240 × 3 = 720 and 400 × 2 = 800; since 800 > 720, the two jumbo boxes hold more in total.
feedback: That compares one box of each size instead of the full purchase — three larges vs. two jumbos.
480 comes from 240 × 2 — the large option has THREE boxes, not two.
The totals are right, but 800 is GREATER than 720, so the jumbo option wins the comparison.
hints: Find each TOTAL before comparing.
Which total is greater?

core.prompt: One garden bed is 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. A second bed is 6 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. How much soil fills BOTH beds?
core.explanation: First bed: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Second bed: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Together: 24 + 24 = 48 cubic feet.
feedback: That adds all the dimensions (4+3+2+6+2+2) instead of multiplying within each bed.
24 cubic feet is only ONE bed — the problem asks for both.
That multiplies the two bed volumes (24 × ... ) too far — you ADD the volumes of the parts, you don't double the total.
hints: Find each bed's volume separately, then combine.
Add the two volumes.

core.prompt: The group found the volume by decomposing the garden into prisms and adding. Why would they compute it a SECOND, different way?
choices: Because the first way is always wrong
To get a bigger number for the soil order
If both ways give the same answer, the solution is accurate
Because volume changes each time you measure it
core.explanation: The book models exactly this: two different decompositions both gave 48 cubic feet, so the solutions match and the answer is accurate.
feedback: The first way can be perfectly correct — the second way CONFIRMS it rather than replaces it.
Checking is about accuracy, not inflating the answer — both ways should give the SAME number.
The garden's volume is fixed — what could vary is our calculation, which is why we check it.
hints: What did the two solutions in the lesson have in common?
The solutions were the same for both ways.
Matching answers mean the calculation is accurate.

choices: “I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal than the three large boxes.”
core.explanation: A conjecture is a mathematical claim you believe but have not yet proven — the jumbo-box claim needs an argument to back it up.
feedback: That is a computed fact, already verified — nothing left to prove.
That is a definition, true by agreement rather than something to test.
That is a plain event from the story, not a mathematical claim to defend.
hints: A conjecture still needs proving.
Which statement says 'I think' about something checkable?
Which one would you build an argument FOR?

core.prompt: A student recommends the three large boxes because the cereal stays fresher — each box is open for less time. Is this argument convincing? Explain.
core.explanation: It is somewhat convincing because it uses a real reason that matters to Yuzuki, not just volume. But it would be stronger with evidence — like how long a box stays fresh once opened. An argument can be convincing without equations if the reasoning is clear.

core.explanation: $3.75 × 4 = $15.00. Change from $50: $35.00. A negative result means more money is needed.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

stretch.prompt: Apply — What Time Is It? The new year starts at midnight on January 1st. What time will it be 2,022 minutes after midnight?
stretch.explanation: 2,022 ÷ 60 = 33 remainder 42, so 2,022 minutes is 33 hours 42 minutes. That is 24 hours (one full day) plus 9 hours 42 minutes — 9:42 a.m. on January 2.
feedback: That reads 2,022 minutes as 20 hours 22 minutes — but minutes must be DIVIDED by 60, not split by place value.
33 hours is more than one full day, so the clock has rolled past midnight into January 2.
After subtracting the 24-hour day, 9 hours 42 minutes past midnight is morning, not evening.
hints: Divide 2,022 by 60 to get hours and leftover minutes.
33 hours is one full day plus how many hours?

stretch.prompt: How many rides would the tram need for 10,000 passengers, at 80 passengers per ride?
stretch.explanation: 10,000 ÷ 80 = 125 rides. Those rides would take 125 × 12.5 = 1,562.5 minutes.
feedback: 12.5 shifts the decimal one place too far — and 12.5 is also the minutes per ride, a different quantity.
250 divides 10,000 by 40 — that would only carry 40 passengers per ride.
1,250 divides 10,000 by 8 instead of 80.
hints: Split 10,000 into equal groups of 80.
Use the 4,000-passenger answer as an anchor: 4,000 needed 50 rides.

stretch.prompt: The lesson says we make strategic decisions about which tool to use. For the 10-hour round-trip question, would you choose a table of values, a coordinate plane, or an equation? Defend your choice.
stretch.explanation: I would choose the table of values, because I can extend the rows by 35 minutes at a time until I pass 600 minutes, and I can see that 600 lands between 525 and 700. A coordinate plane shows the same ordered pairs visually, and an equation like 35 × t ≤ 600 is fastest — any tool works if it shows the relationship between time and round trips, so the strategic part is picking the one I can read most clearly.

stretch.prompt: A student claims: “Greater box volume ALWAYS means more cereal inside.” Which is the best counterexample?
choices: A large box that costs more than a jumbo box
A jumbo box with more volume that is sold half-filled with air
Two jumbo boxes that are easier to store than three large boxes
A box of a different cereal brand
stretch.explanation: A counterexample must break the claim itself: a bigger box holding less cereal (more air) shows greater volume does not guarantee more cereal.
feedback: Price does not test the claim — the claim links volume to AMOUNT of cereal, not cost.
Storage convenience is a different argument entirely; it says nothing about how much cereal is inside.
Changing the brand changes the product, but does not show a bigger box holding less cereal.
hints: A counterexample must make the claim FALSE in one case.
The claim connects volume to amount of cereal.
Find the case where volume is bigger but cereal is not.

stretch.prompt: The garden needs 48 cubic feet of soil. One decomposition used two prisms of 24 cubic feet each. Which of these is ANOTHER decomposition of the same garden volume?
stretch.explanation: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 and 4 × 2 × 2 = 16, and 32 + 16 = 48 cubic feet — the same total by a different split.
feedback: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 and 3 × 3 × 2 = 18 give 45 cubic feet, not 48.
4 × 4 × 2 = 32 twice gives 64 cubic feet, not 48.
6 × 4 × 2 = 48 and 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 give 56 cubic feet, not 48.
hints: Compute each prism's volume, then add.
The parts must total exactly 48.

stretch.prompt: Another garden bed design is also being considered. What information would you need to compare the two designs, and how would you argue for the one you recommend?
stretch.explanation: I would need the dimensions of each design so I could compute both volumes in cubic feet. Then I would build my argument with equations — the volumes — and with words, like which design fits the space better or is easier to reach. I would state my recommendation and defend it with both kinds of evidence.

stretch.explanation: $4.00 × 4 = $16.00. Change from $50: $34.00. A negative result means more money is needed.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
